args.text: [lane-ibis] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Users are sent to old addresses after a server moves, causing outages or errors. (2) Failover is slow, because traffic keeps going to a broken server until the cache expires. (3) A forged or poisoned answer stays in the cache longer, so harm from it lasts longer. Lifetime figures: unknown.

[lane-ibis] Idempotent retries matter because a request that fails or times out may still have worked, so the sender cannot tell whether to try again. If repeating the request gives the same result as doing it once, retrying is safe and avoids double charges, duplicate orders or other repeated effects.

[lane-ibis] Two trade-offs of using UUIDv7 (universally unique identifier, version 7) as a primary key: (1) Values are ordered by time, so inserts land close together in the index, which is kinder than fully random identifiers, but the key reveals roughly when each row was created. (2) It is 128 bits wide, so keys and indexes take more space than a plain integer key.

[lane-ibis] A write-ahead log is a record that a database writes to disk before it changes the main data, so each change is saved first as a short entry. If the system crashes, it replays the log to recover completed changes and to undo unfinished ones, which keeps the data consistent.

[lane-ibis] (1) Results stay comparable: if the client changes between runs, a faster or slower result might come from the new client rather than the thing you are measuring. (2) Results can be repeated: others can rerun the test later with the same client and get the same behaviour, so the numbers can be checked.

[lane-ibis] Backpressure is a way for a queue to tell the senders to slow down when the workers cannot keep up, for example by making them wait or by refusing new items. This stops the queue from growing without limit, which would otherwise use up memory and make everything slower.

[lane-ibis] Two ways a cron job can run twice: (1) the same job is set up on two machines, or in two places on one machine, so both start it at the same time; (2) a run takes longer than the gap between runs, so the next run starts before the first has finished. One guard: take a lock before starting work, for example a lock file or a database lock, and exit at once if another run already holds it.

[lane-ibis] A tombstone is a small marker saved in place of a deleted item, saying that the item was removed and when. It is needed because if a copy were simply erased, another copy that missed the deletion could send the old item back and bring it back to life. Tombstones are kept for an agreed period, then cleared away once all copies have seen them.

[lane-ibis] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than properly failing: (1) It gives different results on the same code, passing on one run and failing on the next with no change made. (2) It fails only under certain conditions, such as when run alongside other tests, at a certain time, or on a busy machine, and passes when run alone or run again.

[lane-ibis] A lease-based lock gives one holder the lock for a set time, after which it runs out and another holder may take it. This depends on every machine agreeing roughly what the time is. If the holder's clock runs slow, it thinks it still has the lock after others see it expire, so two holders act at once. If a checking machine's clock runs fast, it may free the lock too early. Either way the lock's promise of one holder at a time is broken.
